title: Prohibition on Tethering Dogs to Stationary Objects; Heavy Fines and Penalties
summary: Prohibits tethering, fastening, chaining, tying, or restraining a dog to a dog house, tree, fence, or other stationary object, with narrow exceptions (e.g. while performing an activity with the person or a pulley run for up to 3 hours in a 24-hour period). Violations are punishable as infractions with escalating fines or as misdemeanors punishable by a fine of up to $1,000, imprisonment in county jail up to six months, or both.
verbatim_text:
(a) No person shall tether, fasten, chain, tie, or restrain a dog, or cause a dog to be tethered, fastened, chained, tied, or restrained, to a dog house, tree, fence, or any other stationary object.
(b) A person may tether a dog with a handheld leash for the purpose of walking the dog, or during lawful camping, training, or herding, or while actively working with the dog.
(d) A person who violates this section is guilty of an infraction or a misdemeanor. An infraction is punishable by a fine not to exceed two hundred fifty dollars ($250) per dog. A misdemeanor is punishable by a fine not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000) per dog, by imprisonment in a county jail for not more than six months, or by both that fine and imprisonment.

title: Municipal Authority for Dog Control, Leash Mandates, and Licensing
summary: Authorizes California boards of supervisors and city councils to enact local animal control ordinances, including mandatory leash laws for dogs in public places, dog licensing, and impoundment of animals running at large. California state law delegates public dog-walking leash requirements to city and county municipal codes (e.g., Los Angeles County Code § 10.32.010, SF Health Code § 40), where fines for walking dogs off-leash typically range from $100 to over $500.
verbatim_text:
(a) The board of supervisors of any county or the governing body of any city may provide for the registration, licensing, and impounding of all dogs within their jurisdiction, and may enact ordinances regulating the running at large of dogs, including leash requirements on public streets, sidewalks, and parks.
(b) Under Section 31401, violation of any provision of this division or any local ordinance enacted pursuant thereto is an infraction punishable by a fine specified by municipal or county code.

title: Strict Liability for Dog Bites in Public Places
summary: Establishes that the owner of any dog is strictly liable for damages suffered by any person bitten by the dog while in a public place or lawfully in a private place (including the property of the dog owner), regardless of the former viciousness of the dog or the owner's prior knowledge of such viciousness. There is no 'one-free-bite' rule in California.
verbatim_text: (a) The owner of any dog is liable for the damages suffered by any person who is bitten by the dog while in a public place or lawfully in a private place, including the property of the owner of the dog, regardless of the former viciousness of the dog or the owner's knowledge of such viciousness. A person is lawfully upon the private property of such owner within the meaning of this section when he is on such property in the performance of any duty imposed upon him by the laws of this state or by the laws or postal regulations of the United States, or when he is on such property upon the invitation, express or implied, of the owner.

title: Equal Access Rights for Service and Guide Dogs in Housing and Public Areas
summary: Guarantees individuals with disabilities full and equal access to all public accommodations, transportation, and residential housing. Prohibits landlords and businesses from refusing tenancy or charging extra fees or security deposits for trained guide dogs, signal dogs, or service dogs.
verbatim_text:
(a) (1) Individuals with disabilities or medical conditions have the same right as the general public to the full and free use of the streets, highways, sidewalks, walkways, public buildings, medical facilities, and other public facilities.
(b) (1) Individuals with disabilities shall be entitled to full and equal access to all housing accommodations offered for rent, lease, or compensation.
(2) Nothing in this subdivision shall require a person renting, leasing, or providing for compensation real property to modify his or her property, except that a person renting property shall permit a tenant to keep a specially trained guide dog, signal dog, or service dog without extra charge.

title: Prohibition Against Leaving Animals Unattended in Motor Vehicles
summary: Prohibits leaving or confining an animal in any unattended motor vehicle under conditions that endanger the health or well-being of an animal due to heat, cold, lack of adequate ventilation, or lack of food or water. Violations are punishable by a fine of $100 for a first infraction, and up to $500 and six months imprisonment if the animal suffers great bodily injury.
verbatim_text:
(a) A person shall not leave or confine an animal in any unattended motor vehicle under conditions that endanger the health or well-being of an animal due to heat, cold, lack of adequate ventilation, or lack of food or water, or other circumstances that could reasonably be expected to cause suffering, disability, or death to the animal.
(b) (1) A first conviction for violation of this section is an infraction punishable by a fine not exceeding one hundred dollars ($100) per animal. If the animal suffers great bodily injury, a violation is punishable by a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars ($500), imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding six months, or both.

title: Tenant Protection Act of 2019 - Mandatory Limits on Rent Increases
summary: Caps annual residential rent increases in California at 5% plus the percentage change in the cost of living (regional CPI), or 10%, whichever is lower. Applies over any 12-month period for covered residential real property. Exempts certain housing such as dormitories, deed-restricted affordable housing, housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years, and single-family homes/condominiums unless owned by a corporate entity (REIT, corporation, or LLC with corporate member) with required statutory disclosure provided to the tenant.
verbatim_text:
(a) (1) Subject to subdivision (b), an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit to more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, of the lowest gross rental rate charged for that dwelling or unit at any time during the 12 months prior to the effective date of the increase.
(2) If the same tenant remains in occupancy over any 12-month period, the gross rental rate shall not be increased in more than two increments over that 12-month period.
(d) This section shall not apply to the following types of residential real properties:
(1) Housing restricted by deed, regulatory restriction, or other recorded document as affordable housing.
(2) Dormitories constructed and maintained in connection with higher education institutions.
(3) Housing that has been issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years.
(4) Residential real property that is alienable separate from the title to any other dwelling unit (e.g. single-family residences or condominiums), provided that the owner is not a real estate investment trust, a corporation, or an LLC in which at least one member is a corporation, and the tenant has been provided written notice of this exemption.

title: Notice Required for Change in Terms of Lease or Rent Increase
summary: Requires landlords to give written notice before changing terms of a periodic tenancy or increasing rent. If the proposed rent increase is 10% or less of the lowest amount charged during the preceding 12 months, at least 30 days' advance written notice is required. If the proposed rent increase is more than 10%, at least 90 days' advance written notice is required.
verbatim_text:
(b) (1) In all leases of a residential dwelling, or of any interest therein, from week to week, month to month, or other period less than a month, the landlord may increase the amount of rent to be paid upon delivered written notice.
(2) If the proposed rent increase is 10 percent or less of the rental amount charged to that tenant at any time during the 12 months prior to the effective date of the increase, either in and of itself or when combined with any other rent increases in that 12-month period, the notice shall be delivered at least 30 days prior to the effective date of the increase.
(3) If the proposed rent increase is greater than 10 percent of the rental amount charged to that tenant at any time during the 12 months prior to the effective date of the increase, the notice shall be delivered at least 90 days prior to the effective date of the increase.

title: Residential Security Deposits; Itemized Statement and Return Deadlines
summary: Governs security deposits for California residential leases. Requires the landlord to return the unused deposit and furnish an itemized statement of deductions with receipts within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates. Limits permissible deductions to unpaid rent, cleaning to return unit to move-in condition, and repair of damages beyond normal wear and tear. Bad-faith retention can subject landlord to statutory damages of up to twice the deposit amount.
verbatim_text:
(g) (1) No later than 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, the landlord shall furnish the tenant, by personal delivery or by first-class mail, postage prepaid, a copy of an itemized statement indicating the basis for, and the amount of, any security received and the disposition of the security, and shall return any remaining portion of the security to the tenant.
(2) Along with the itemized statement, the landlord shall submit copies of documents showing charges incurred and actually paid by the landlord to repair or clean the premises.
(l) The bad faith claim or retention by a landlord of the security or any portion thereof in violation of this section may subject the landlord to statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security, in addition to actual damages.

title: Tenant Protection Act of 2019 - Mandatory Just Cause Eviction Protections
summary: Prohibits landlords from terminating tenancies of covered tenants who have occupied residential property for 12 months or more without at-fault just cause or no-fault just cause stated in the written notice. For no-fault evictions (such as owner move-in or substantial remodel), the landlord must provide relocation assistance equal to one month of rent.
verbatim_text:
(a) After a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate the tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.
(b) For purposes of this section, 'just cause' includes At-Fault Just Cause (e.g. default in payment of rent, breach of a material lease term, nuisance) and No-Fault Just Cause (e.g. intent to occupy by owner or owner's spouse, domestic partner, children, or parents, withdrawal of property from rental market under Ellis Act, substantial rehabilitation).

title: Implied Warranty of Habitability - Untenantable Dwellings
summary: Establishes baseline standards for a residential dwelling to be deemed tenantable. Requires effective waterproofing and weather protection of roof and exterior walls, operational plumbing, hot and cold running water, heating facilities, electrical lighting and wiring maintained in good working order, clean and sanitary buildings free from debris, rodents, and vermin, adequate garbage receptacles, and safe floors, stairways, and railings.
verbatim_text:
(a) A dwelling shall be deemed untenantable for purposes of Section 1941 if it substantially lacks any of the following affirmative standard characteristics:
(1) Effective waterproofing and weather protection of roof and exterior walls, including unbroken windows and doors.
(2) Plumbing or gas facilities that conformed to applicable law in effect at the time of installation, maintained in good working order.
(3) A water supply approved under applicable law that produces hot and cold running water.
(4) Heating facilities that conformed with applicable law at the time of installation, maintained in good working order.
(5) Electrical lighting, with wiring and electrical equipment that conformed with applicable law.
(6) Building, grounds, and appurtenances at the time of the commencement of the lease or rental agreement, and all areas under control of the landlord, kept clean, sanitary, and free from all accumulations of debris, filth, rubbish, garbage, rodents, and vermin.

title: Tenant Repair and Deduct Remedy
summary: Permits a tenant, after giving written or oral notice to the landlord of dilapidations rendering premises untenantable, to repair the defect and deduct the costs from rent (up to one month's rent) if the landlord neglects to do so within a reasonable time (presumed to be 30 days, or sooner in urgent cases). Remedy can be used no more than twice in any 12-month period.
verbatim_text:
(a) If within a reasonable time after written or oral notice to the landlord or the landlord's agent of dilapidations rendering the premises untenantable which the landlord ought to repair, the landlord neglects to do so, the tenant may repair the dilapidations and deduct the expenses of the repair from the rent when due, or the tenant may vacate the premises.
(b) For the purposes of this section, if the tenant acts to repair and deduct after the 30th day following notice, the tenant is presumed to have acted after a reasonable time. The tenant cannot invoke this remedy more than twice in any 12-month period.

title: Immediate Payment of Wages Upon Employer Discharge or Termination
summary: Requires that if an employer discharges an employee, all earned and unpaid wages, including accrued and unused vacation or PTO, are due and payable immediately at the time and place of termination.
verbatim_text: (a) If an employer discharges an employee, the wages earned and unpaid at the time of discharge are due and payable immediately. An employer having a seasonal employment involved in curing, canning, or drying any variety of perishable fruit, fish or vegetables, shall pay wages within a reasonable time as provided by regulation.

title: Payment of Wages Upon Employee Resignation or Quitting
summary: Requires that if an employee resigns without giving at least 72 hours' prior notice, their wages must be made available no later than 72 hours after quitting. If the employee gave at least 72 hours' advance notice of quitting, wages are due on the last day of work.
verbatim_text: (a) If an employee not having a written contract for a definite period quits his or her employment, his or her wages shall become due and payable not later than 72 hours thereafter, unless the employee has given 72 hours previous notice of his or her intention to quit, in which case the employee is entitled to his or her wages at the time of quitting.

title: Waiting Time Penalties for Willful Failure to Pay Final Wages
summary: Imposes statutory waiting time penalties if an employer willfully fails to timely pay wages upon termination under Section 201 or Section 202. The employee's wages continue as a penalty at the same daily rate until paid or until an action is commenced, up to a maximum of 30 days.
verbatim_text: (a) If an employer willfully fails to pay, without abatement or reduction, in accordance with Sections 201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.5, 201.6, 201.8, 201.9, 202, and 202.5, any wages of an employee who is discharged or who quits, the wages of the employee shall continue as a penalty from the due date thereof at the same rate until paid or until an action therefor is commenced; but the wages shall not continue for more than 30 days.

title: Mandatory Itemized Wage Statements and Recordkeeping
summary: Mandates that employers furnish an accurate, itemized wage statement showing gross wages, total hours worked, all deductions, net wages, dates of pay period, employee name and last four of SSN, employer name and legal address, and all applicable hourly rates in effect during the pay period.
verbatim_text: (a) An employer, semimonthly or at the time of each payment of wages, shall furnish to his or her employee, either as a detachable part of the check, draft, or voucher paying the employee's wages, or separately if wages are paid by personal check or cash, an accurate itemized statement in writing showing (1) gross wages earned, (2) total hours worked by the employee, (3) the number of piece-rate units earned, (4) all deductions, (5) net wages earned, (6) the inclusive dates of the period for which the employee is paid, (7) the name of the employee and only the last four digits of his or her social security number, (8) the name and address of the legal entity that is the employer, and (9) all applicable hourly rates in effect during the pay period.

title: California Overtime Compensation Standard
summary: Requires payment of one and one-half times the regular rate of pay for work in excess of 8 hours up to and including 12 hours in any workday, and for the first 8 hours on the seventh consecutive day of work. Requires double time for hours worked in excess of 12 hours in any workday, and for all hours worked in excess of 8 hours on the seventh consecutive day of work.
verbatim_text: (a) Eight hours of labor constitutes a day's work. Any work in excess of eight hours in one workday and any work in excess of 40 hours in any one workweek and the first eight hours worked on the seventh day of work in any one workweek shall be compensated at the rate of no less than one and one-half times the regular rate of pay for an employee. Any work in excess of 12 hours in one day shall be compensated at the rate of no less than twice the regular rate of pay for an employee.

title: Small Claims Court Jurisdiction and Monetary Limits
summary: Defines the jurisdiction of California small claims courts. Individuals (natural persons) can bring claims for money damages up to $12,500. Corporations, LLCs, and other entities are limited to claims of $6,250 or less. Lawyers generally cannot represent parties in California small claims hearings.
verbatim_text:
(a) The small claims court has jurisdiction in the following actions:
(1) For recovery of money, if the amount of the demand does not exceed the jurisdictional limit. In actions brought by a natural person, the jurisdictional limit is twelve thousand five hundred dollars ($12,500). In actions brought by an entity, the limit is six thousand two hundred fifty dollars ($6,250).
(b) The small claims court may grant equitable relief in the form of rescission, restitution, reformation, and specific performance, in lieu of, or in addition to, money damages.

title: Corporal Punishment or Child Abuse; Reasonable Discipline Exception
summary: Prohibits any person from willfully inflicting upon any child any cruel or inhuman corporal punishment or injury resulting in a traumatic condition. Under California common law and statutory interpretation, parents have a limited privilege to administer reasonable, non-excessive corporal punishment for disciplinary purposes, but physical discipline that causes traumatic injury, excessive harm, or unreasonable force constitutes a felony or misdemeanor under Penal Code § 273d.
verbatim_text:
(a) Any person who willfully inflicts upon any child any cruel or inhuman corporal punishment or injury resulting in a traumatic condition is guilty of a felony, and upon conviction thereof shall be punished by imprisonment pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1170 for two, four, or six years, or in a county jail for not more than one year, or by a fine of up to six thousand dollars ($6,000) or by both that fine and imprisonment.
(b) Upon a second or subsequent conviction, the court shall impose an additional sentence enhancement.

title: Battery Defined - Unlawful Physical Force
summary: Defines battery as any willful and unlawful use of force or violence upon the person of another. Under Penal Code § 243, simple battery is punishable by a fine not exceeding $2,000, or by imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding six months, or both.
verbatim_text: A battery is any willful and unlawful use of force or violence upon the person of another. Under Section 243, battery is punishable by a fine not exceeding two thousand dollars ($2,000), or by imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding six months, or by both that fine and imprisonment.

title: Unlawful Possession of Controlled Substances
summary: Prohibits possession of specified controlled substances (including narcotics and unprescribed prescription drugs) without a valid written prescription. Under California Proposition 47, simple possession is generally punishable as a misdemeanor by imprisonment in a county jail for up to one year, subject to diversion programs (e.g. Penal Code § 1000).
verbatim_text: (a) Except as otherwise provided in this division, every person who possesses any controlled substance specified in subdivision (b), (c), (e), or paragraph (1) of subdivision (f) of Section 11054, or specified in paragraph (14), (15), or (20) of subdivision (b) of Section 11055, unless upon the written prescription of a physician, dentist, podiatrist, or veterinarian, shall be punished by imprisonment in a county jail for not more than one year.
